title: Triage messaging scaffold: engineering roles
content:
Purpose
This note is a compact, runbook-style scaffold for SDRs/AMs and solution engineers to align messaging across three technical personas: ML Engineers, Backend Engineers, and Platform Teams. Goal: quickly surface the dominant engineering levers (latency, cost, observability, integration effort) and give tight talk tracks, demo hooks, and rebuttals that map to real engineering decision criteria.

How to use
- Read the one-liners for each persona before a call.
- Pick 1–2 demo hooks and 1 quick benchmark to cite.
- Use the qualifying questions to determine whether to escalate to a Solutions Engineer or propose a Dedicated/Private evaluation.

Overview summary (for executives)
- ML Engineers: care about model fidelity, reproducibility, eval guardrails, and being able to iterate on prompts and model variants quickly in dev and staging. They want reproducible inference and a clear story for model rollouts.
- Backend Engineers: prioritize API stability, latency SLOs, batching behavior, and cost predictability at scale. They evaluate throughput, retry semantics, and easy SDKs/observability for production endpoints.
- Platform Teams: focus on operational controls, multi-tenant isolation, autoscaling policies, private deployment options, and governance (KMS, audit logs, network controls). They are buying for org-wide standardization and risk reduction.

Persona one-liners (use as opener)
- ML Engineer: "You want to iterate on model variants with minimal friction — we give reproducible inference, model versioning, and token-level quality metrics so you can ship updates safely."
- Backend Engineer: "You need predictable latency and cost as traffic grows — we provide per-route SLAs, autoscaling policies, and transparent token/cost telemetry to avoid surprise bills."
- Platform Team: "You need uniform enforcement of security and operational policies — we offer VPC/private deployments, KMS integration, and rollout controls to make inference a platform service."

Top priorities & proof points to cite
- Latency SLOs: cite typical 95p latencies for common families (e.g., 80–250ms for small LLMs on dedicated GPU pools) and fallback routing to keep p95 under SLA.
- Cost controls: show token-level chargeback, batching and prefix cache savings (examples: 30–60% cost reduction on conversational workloads with prefix caching).
- Reliability: describe model variant fallback and cross-region routing to avoid outages during regional capacity constraints.
- Reproducibility: model pins, deterministic seed support, tokenized request/response logging for audit.

Qualifying questions (quick)
- ML Eng: "How often do you iterate on model weights or prompt templates in prod? What percent of responses do you evaluate with golden prompts?"
- Backend Eng: "What's your 95th percentile latency requirement? How many qps do you expect per endpoint at peak?"
- Platform: "Do you have an internal marketplace for inference? What are your encryption/KMS requirements? Is VPC connectivity required?"

Demo hooks (pick 1 per call)
- Live prompt roll-forward: show deploying a model version + canary traffic routing + rollback in the Console (ML Eng + Platform). Emphasize quick revert and audit trail.
- Latency profile explorer: run a synthetic multi-tenant load plan and show per-route p50/p95 and token breakdown (Backend + Platform).
- Cost delta with caching: replay a chat traffic sample with and without prefix/KV caching and show % cost change and latency difference (ML + Backend).
- Private connect: walkthrough of VPC peering setup and KMS key configuration (Platform).

Persona-specific talk tracks, objections, and quick rebuttals
- ML Engineer
  - Focus: model fidelity, evals, iteration speed, deterministic outputs.
  - Talk track: "We integrate with your eval harness and track drift/regressions at the prompt-set level. You can pin models per route and run automated A/B rollouts to test quality impact."
  - Likely objections: "Quantized models reduce quality" -> Rebuttal: "We provide model recommendations based on your workload distribution and A/B evals; for many workloads Q4-8 quantization is indistinguishable when tuned and reduces cost by Xx."
  - Rebuttal: "I can’t reproduce inference results" -> "We store token-level inputs/outputs, model version pins, and runtime seed metadata so experiments are reproducible across environments."

- Backend Engineer
  - Focus: latency, stable API semantics, retries, cost predictability.
  - Talk track: "Our SDKs provide request-level timeouts, idempotency keys, and token/latency billing breakdowns so you can budget and instrument like a standard backend service."
  - Likely objections: "We can’t risk increased p95" -> Rebuttal: "We offer tiered routing to low-latency dedicated pools + graceful fallback to regional compatible variants to preserve p95 under load."
  - Likely objections: "SDKs are noisy or heavy" -> Rebuttal: "We have lightweight HTTP SDKs, language clients, and OpenAPI for quick integration. You can adopt per-route throttles and retry strategies without code churn."

- Platform Team
  - Focus: governance, isolation, onboarding at scale.
  - Talk track: "Redwood is an inference runtime you can standardize on: RBAC, audit logs, KMS, and per-team quotas make it a drop-in platform service."
  - Likely objections: "We’re worried about vendor lock-in" -> Rebuttal: "We support model portability and exportable configs; Dedicated/Private options let you control infra while keeping the same operational surface."
  - Likely objections: "Hard to certify for compliance" -> Rebuttal: "We provide audit-ready logs, optional HSM integrations, and SOC-style documentation for enterprise customers."

Competitive notes (short)
- Public cloud vendor endpoints: good for breadth but often lack inference-level batching/caching optimizations, and their pricing/latency tradeoffs can be opaque for tokenized workloads. Use: position Redwood on predictable unit economics and inference-specific optimizations.
- Open-source self-hosted stacks: attractive for control; raise concerns about long-term maintenance, kernel selection, and ops cost. Use: position Redwood on offloading operational toil (patches, performance tuning, fallback routing).
- Single-model API vendors: simpler API but limited deployment modes. Use: highlight Redwood’s unified surface across hosted/dedicated/private + rollout/observability features.

Success metrics to track post-demo
- Time to first inference in staging (target < 1 hour for hosted API).
- p95 latency before/after caching or model variant change.
- Token cost delta on pilot traffic (show baseline vs Redwood-optimized settings).
- Number of critical incidents avoided due to fallback routing during pilot.

Suggested leave-behinds and assets
- 1-page: "Engineering evaluation checklist" with fields: latency target, throughput, KMS requirements, SLO windows, eval dataset link.
- Demo recording snippet: 3–4 minute clip of canary rollout + rollback.
- Cost/latency worksheet: simple table to paste sample qps and get modeled token cost for a month.

Open questions & experiments to run
- Measure quality delta for quantized vs full models on typical prompt-set (ask ML team to pick 200 golden prompts).
- Run a stress test to determine the auto-scaling curve and cold-start characteristics for dedicated pools.

Notes to SEs: keep it pragmatic and focused. Before any technical deep-dive, ask the qualifying questions and pick a single demo hook that addresses the prospect's top pain. Avoid trying to show everything — engineers respect focused, measurable claims.
